slides.heading: Python Functions in Practice
narration: Welcome to this short lesson on Python functions.
We will cover how to define a function, how parameters and arguments work, what return values are, and how variable scope decides where a name can be seen.

slides.heading: Defining a function
narration: You define a function with the def keyword, a name, parentheses, and a colon.
The indented lines underneath are the body.
Defining a function only stores it. The body runs each time you call the function, for example by writing greet followed by parentheses.

slides.heading: Parameters and arguments
slides.code:
def area(width, height=1):
    return width * height

area(3, 4)   # 12
area(5)      # 5
narration: Parameters are the names inside the parentheses of the definition. Arguments are the values you pass when you call it.
Python matches positional arguments from left to right, or you can pass keyword arguments by name.
A parameter can have a default value, so the caller may leave it out.

slides.heading: Return values
narration: The return statement sends a value back to the caller and ends the function immediately.
If a function never reaches a return statement, it returns None.
Remember that printing a value is not the same as returning it. You can also return several values, which Python packs into a tuple.

slides.heading: Variable scope: LEGB
slides.code:
count = 10

def bump():
    count = 1
    return count

bump()  # 1, global count is still 10
narration: Scope decides where a name can be seen. Variables assigned inside a function are local to it.
Python looks names up in the order local, enclosing, global, and built in.
Assigning to a name inside a function creates a new local variable, so the global value stays unchanged.

slides.heading: Recap
narration: To recap: functions give logic a name, take inputs through parameters, and hand results back with return.
Keep them small and avoid changing global state, and they will be easy to reuse and test. Thanks for watching.

slides.heading: Introduction
narration: This is an audio lesson on the basics of the SQL SELECT statement.
SQL is the language used to ask questions of relational databases, where data lives in tables made of rows and columns.

slides.heading: SELECT and FROM
narration: Every query starts with SELECT, followed by the columns you want, and FROM, followed by the table.
For example, select name comma email from students returns two columns for every row in the students table.
Select star returns every column, which is handy for exploring but wasteful in production code.

slides.heading: Filtering with WHERE
narration: The WHERE clause keeps only the rows that match a condition.
For example, where enrolled year equals twenty twenty six keeps only students who enrolled this year.
You can combine conditions with and, or, and not.

slides.heading: ORDER BY and LIMIT
narration: ORDER BY sorts the result by one or more columns, in ascending order unless you add the keyword descending.
LIMIT caps the number of rows returned, which is useful for top ten style questions.
Put together, a query can select names from students, filter by year, order by last name, and limit the result to ten rows.

slides.heading: Recap
narration: To recap: SELECT chooses columns, FROM chooses the table, WHERE filters rows, ORDER BY sorts them, and LIMIT caps how many come back.
That covers the core of most everyday queries. Thanks for listening.
